text: Compound past dollar costs to today's money: a dollar spent earlier was worth more (interest)
description: Felix 2026-11-23, with the decision to store realized harness cost in USD (675fce29): money gets cheaper over time, so a dollar spent back then was worth more, like interest. When realized costs from different months are summed or compared with estimates, compound each to today's money: cost_today = cost_then · (1 + r)^(days/365). r is the same annual rate the model already uses for cost of capital (ANNUAL_DISCOUNT_RATE, 10%), or a per-project setting. It applies wherever past USD costs are added up: an idea's realized total, a branch's aggregated cost, the calibration script. The stored value stays the nominal dollars at the time; compounding is computed, so git keeps the raw facts. Pulls the opposite way of the intelligence-growth discount (sibling idea): interest makes past dollars count more, cheaper intelligence makes past work count less.

status.comment: Modelled 2026-11-24 (before building): 21 ideas carry realizedCostUsd, the oldest from 2026-11-08, so the data spans ~16 days. At r = 10%/yr compounding multiplies a cost by 1.0042 at 16 days, 1.0079 at 30, 1.049 at 6 months, 1.10 at a year: far below the spread of the cost estimates it would be compared with. The opposite pull, the intelligence-growth discount (760d59dd), is 10-100x larger at every age (g=4/yr: ×0.94 at 16 days, ×0.50 at 6 months; g=10: ×0.90, ×0.32). Decision (reversible): don't build interest compounding on its own yet; build it as the second factor inside 760d59dd's one 'cost in today's money' function, cost_today = cost_then · (1+r)^(t) · g^(−t), so both share the git-date lookup from the design note above. Hypothesis that could fail: until the oldest realized cost is ~6 months old, compounding changes no idea's priority rank.
